newsitem.title: FRANCE: French leaders take election battle to the streets.
newsitem.headline: French leaders take election battle to the streets.

text.p: Political leaders prepared to take their election battle to the streets and people of France on Thursday for what is expected to be a short but bruising campaign.

Gaullist Prime Minister Alain Juppe and Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin were both to hold their first public rallies and walkabouts in the campaign, which will culminate with two rounds of voting to elect a new parliament on May 25 and June 1.
Juppe will be in the rough and tumble Mediterranean port of Marseille, while Jospin will tour several troubled outer Paris suburbs.
Juppe told campaign workers late on Wednesday he hoped the campaign "will be joyful, even if I know it will be brutal."

So far, the campaign, launched on Monday by President Jacques Chirac when he announced the snap election, has been waged in a battle of communiques and in interviews largely centred on such learned issues as the terms for a single European currency.
It was unlikely party leaders would try to bring the debate over such questions to street level, where worries are more likely to focus on unemployment, immigration and crime.
The first opinion poll taken since Chirac called the election suggested the ruling centre-right coalition would win comfortably with a sharply reduced majority.
But another survey found most voters expected to be hit by further austerity measures after the election.
In a volley of television statements late on Tuesday, former Socialist prime minister Laurent Fabius said: "The construction of Europe will have to be re-thought with social issues more in mind."

Former conservative prime minister Edouard Balladur, who will take part in the government's campaign despite unsuccessfully challenging Chirac for the presidency, said France should reduce its budget deficit to meet the criteria for joining the European currency.

The executive European Commission gave the government a boost by forecasting France would pass the key test to qualify -- holding the public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product both this year and next.

But the International Monetary Fund gave credence to Socialist warnings of a fresh wave of austerity to come by saying France needed to take more measures to cut its deficit durably below three percent.
In another setback for Juppe, the IMF forecast unemployment would continue to rise to more than 13 percent by mid-1997 from a record 12.8 percent in March.
A poll by the CSA institute suggested the centre-right will win 332 of the 555 seats in metropolitan France to 222 for the combined left-wing opposition and one for the far-right National Front.
The coalition holds 464 of the 577 seats in the outgoing assembly, including most of the 22 seats in overseas departments and territories which are not covered by opinion polls.
